passageTitle: The Long Life of Roman Concrete
note: AI-authored original IELTS Academic Reading passage for the morning-quiz bank (2026-07, batch v2). Not from a past examination paper. Factual content on Roman concrete (opus caementicium), pozzolanic reaction, marine Al-tobermorite growth (Jackson et al. 2017) and the lime-clast self-healing / hot-mixing hypothesis (Masic et al., MIT, 2023). ~780 words; 13 questions across matching-information, TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN, sentence completion and flow-chart completion.
passage:
Paragraph A
In the heart of Rome stands the Pantheon, its vast concrete dome unbroken after nearly nineteen centuries. No steel bars run through it; no modern additive protects it. Ordinary concrete of the kind poured today would be crumbling long before reaching such an age, its surfaces spalling and its inner reinforcement rusting away within decades. That a material mixed by hand two thousand years ago should outlast the products of modern chemistry has long puzzled engineers, and only recently have laboratories begun to explain how the Romans achieved it.

Paragraph B
Roman concrete was made from three main ingredients: lime, a coarse aggregate of rubble or broken stone, and — most importantly — volcanic ash. The finest ash was dug from deposits near the town of Pozzuoli, on the Bay of Naples, and the material took the name pozzolana from that place. When this ash was combined with lime and water, it triggered what chemists now call the pozzolanic reaction, in which the ash and the lime slowly bind together into a tough, stone-like cement. It was this reaction, rather than the lime alone, that gave the mixture its strength.

Paragraph C
The Romans reserved some of their boldest use of the material for the sea. They poured concrete directly into wooden forms sunk beneath the waves to build harbour walls and breakwaters. Here the contrast with modern practice is starkest of all. Sea water is the enemy of today's concrete, working into every crack and corroding the steel within until the structure fails. Roman marine concrete did the opposite: exposed to the same salt water for centuries, it did not decay but grew steadily harder and more solid.

Paragraph D
The reason, researchers discovered, lies in a slow chemical conversation between the concrete and the sea. As sea water percolated through the material, it dissolved parts of the volcanic ash and allowed rare interlocking crystals to grow in the spaces left behind. These crystals, one of which is a mineral called Al-tobermorite, knitted the concrete together from within, reinforcing it exactly where ordinary concrete would weaken. The very process that destroys modern harbour walls was, in the Roman recipe, a means of repair. The effect was slow, unfolding over decades and centuries rather than years, which is one reason it went unrecognised for so long.

Paragraph E
One feature of Roman concrete had puzzled observers for years: it is dotted with small white lumps, a few millimetres across, known as lime clasts. For a long time these were read as a sign of careless work — evidence that the ancient builders had simply failed to mix their materials thoroughly. Because they seemed like flaws, many studies passed over them without comment. Such pale flecks appear in Roman concrete at sites across the former empire, so ordinary a feature that for decades few researchers thought to ask what they were for.

Paragraph F
In 2023 a team of researchers proposed a very different reading. They argued that the lime clasts were not a mistake but the key to the concrete's ability to heal itself. The clasts, they suggested, were formed by 'hot mixing' — combining the ingredients with quicklime, the raw and reactive form of lime, rather than with lime that had already been slaked in water. Hot mixing left tiny reservoirs of reactive lime scattered through the finished concrete. Quicklime reacts violently when it meets water, giving off heat, and the team suspects that mixing at such high temperatures also helped the concrete set more quickly and encouraged useful compounds to form that cooler, gentler mixing would never have produced.

Paragraph G
The advantage of these reservoirs appears whenever the concrete cracks. If a crack opens and rainwater seeps in, the water reaches a nearby lime clast and dissolves it. The dissolved lime then re-forms as calcium carbonate, which crystallises inside the crack and seals it shut before it can spread. To test the idea, the team cast concrete by the hot-mixing method, deliberately cracked it, and ran water through the gap; within a couple of weeks the crack had closed, while a comparison sample made without the clasts stayed open.

Paragraph H
These discoveries are more than historical curiosities. Modern concrete production is responsible for a large share of the world's carbon emissions, and structures that crack and must be replaced only add to that burden. A concrete that lasts for centuries and mends its own cracks would cut both waste and emissions, and engineers are now testing mixtures that borrow the Roman tricks of pozzolana and hot mixing. There are limits: Roman concrete is weak in tension and cannot simply replace the steel-reinforced concrete of bridges and towers. But as a lesson in building things to last, the two-thousand-year-old recipe still has much to teach.
